_comment: A film, as data. ONE file is the source for both the voice and the camera:
the narration is generated from `say`, and the recorder walks the same list
in the same order, holding each shot for exactly as long as its line takes
to speak. Two files would drift, and a film where the pointer presses the
next button while the sentence is still finishing is worse than no film.
Replace the three demo scenes below with your own. Keep the shape.
How fast the film goes, in ONE place. These three numbers were in three
different files - the pause was written as 800 in record.js and as 0.8 in
assemble.js - and three copies of a number are three chances for the
picture and the voice to drift apart.
lengthScale is Piper's --length-scale: above 1.0 speaks slower. 1.0 was
the first film, which the owner found too fast to follow.
sentenceSilence is Piper's --sentence-silence: breath BETWEEN sentences,
which is most of what makes a voice sound like a person rather than a
list being read out.
pauseSeconds is the gap the recorder holds, and the silence assemble.js
puts between lines. They must be the same number or the film drifts.
Which engine speaks, and in which voice.
kokoro: an 82M model, Apache-2.0, CPU-only, read off its model card on
2026-10-17. Chosen because the owner found Piper mechanical. Its own
VOICES.md grades af_heart A and af_bella A-; the best male voice it offers
is a C+, which is worth knowing before anybody asks for a man's voice.
piper: still supported and still here. It covers far more languages and is
tiny. Set engine to 'piper' and the two piperVoices are used instead.
speed is Kokoro's own multiplier - below 1.0 is slower. Piper's equivalent
is the lengthScale in the pacing block, which is not the same number and
is deliberately kept separate.

The owner listened to four Kokoro voices on 2026-10-17 and chose am_michael. Its own VOICES.md grades that voice C+ against af_heart's A - the owner was told that and chose it anyway, which is his call to make and not Claude's: Claude cannot hear any of them.
Only needed if you use the `screen:<name>` shortcut, and only if your app
has one nav button per screen. %s is the screen's name. Delete this block
and use press: and wait: instead if your app is not shaped like that.

demo.title: <Your app> — what it does
_comment: THE FIVE RULES, each one learned by showing a film to somebody:
1. Say it over something MOVING. A run of still shots longer than 20
seconds is refused outright: nobody watches a static screen being
talked at, however good the words are.
2. Zoom no closer than 2.0x, and ALWAYS zoomOutAfter. A button is
identified by its neighbours, so a tight crop says less than a wide
shot with a ring round it - and a zoom that never releases leaves the
whole line playing over a magnified fragment.
3. One idea per beat. Seven short scenes beat one scene listing seven
things.
4. Only claim what is on the screen. If the line says the record appears,
the film must actually press Save.
5. Keep the examples ordinary. An inflated number is the first thing
somebody in the trade notices, and the last thing they forget.
zoom: what fills the screen. zoomScale: how close (<= 2.0).
zoomOutAfter: pull back once the action is done - this is how the
CONSEQUENCE gets shown. highlightAfter: the ring for that wider shot.
{placeholders} come from video/world.js setUp().

say.en: Welcome to <your app>: one sentence on what it is and who it is for.
say.es: Bienvenido a <su aplicación>: una frase sobre qué es y para quién es.

say.en: Explain how somebody gets an account WHILE the form is being filled in, so the picture is never still.
say.es: Explique cómo se obtiene una cuenta MIENTRAS se rellena el formulario, para que la imagen nunca esté quieta.

say.en: Name the button, say what pressing it does, and let the zoom-out show the result.
say.es: Nombre el botón, diga qué hace al pulsarlo, y deje que el alejamiento muestre el resultado.
